messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was an 18-year-old African American police officer who had come for help after years of feeling as if his own body and mind were always braced for something to go wrong. He grew up in a home where his father’s violence toward his mother was a recurring part of childhood, and one evening in particular had stayed lodged in him with painful clarity: the raised voice from the kitchen, the sudden crash of something hitting the wall, his mother backing into the corner, and his own small body frozen nearby, unable to move or make it stop. When he remembered that night, it did not return as a full story but as a few sharp pictures, each one vivid and separate, and he could feel himself back in the same position he had been in then, shoulders hunched, chest tight, as if his body were replaying the scene before his mind could catch up. What he felt most when the memory came was overwhelming grief. At the same time, he would say with a kind of shame that he did not trust himself anymore, that his reactions since then meant he was going crazy, and that he could not stop bad things from happening to him.

Those beliefs shaped how Kwame moved through the world. He had come to feel that he could not rely on himself to judge danger properly, and that helplessness made him scan every setting for signs that something was about to happen. On patrol, he noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects everywhere—a metal bar beside a doorway, a bottle left on a stoop, a hand disappearing into a pocket—and he avoided unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger. He also became intensely unsettled by unusual silence; a quiet hallway or a room that suddenly went still made him feel that something dangerous was about to happen, as though silence itself were the moment before the blow. Suspicious-looking people, especially those lingering without explanation, triggered the same tension in him, because he had come to believe that if he was not alert at every second, he would be caught off guard. His sense that he could not stop bad things from happening to him kept these habits alive, and the more he looked for danger, the more certain he became that it was everywhere.

As those weeks and months went on, the memories began to surface more easily. A sudden touch from behind in the station corridor could pull him straight back to the old fear, not as an abstract recollection but as a bodily reenactment in which he felt himself folded into the same tense posture he had held as a child. In those moments the pictures of the domestic violence came back in fragments, and with them the grief and the old helplessness. The memory then fed his conviction that he was not steady enough to trust; if his body could be taken over so quickly, he thought, maybe there was something wrong with him. That fear of going crazy made him even more uneasy around physical contact and around any unexpected touch, and he began to flinch when colleagues bumped into him or tapped his shoulder without warning. He also found himself more sensitive to sensations of discomfort in general, because any feeling of unease seemed like the first sign that he was losing control.

The same memory also sharpened his threat monitoring. Once the scene from childhood had been activated, he would spend the rest of the shift watching people’s hands, doorways, and corners, and every suspicious movement felt loaded with intent. He became increasingly wary of unfamiliar places, including parts of the neighborhood he was assigned to patrol, and he would take longer routes if it meant staying in areas where he knew the exits and the likely hazards. The danger he kept imagining reinforced the belief that he could not protect himself, and that belief made the old images come back again and again. By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by this tight loop: a touch, a hush, or a suspicious glance would bring back the same fractured pictures of childhood violence, the grief would rise, and with it the certainty that he was unsafe, unreliable, and one mistake away from something catastrophic. He had finally come because the hypervigilance was starting to affect his work and because he was frightened by how quickly he could be pulled back into that old helpless state. More than anything, he wanted to stop feeling as though danger was always about to break in on him, and he feared that if it did not change, he would spend the rest of his life trapped in the same fear he had felt as a child.
